verdicts.reason: The chapter, approval date and substituted sunset are explicit in the held statute.

The FTC and criminal provisions have commerce limitations; section 3 is not a complete inventory of all consequences.
verdicts.corrected_wording: NIRA section 3(b) makes an approved code the standard of fair competition and treats violations in transactions in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce as unfair methods under the FTC Act; section 3(c) provides equity enforcement; section 3(f) makes violations in such transactions misdemeanors. Section 3(d) permits a prescribed code with the same effect as one approved under 3(a). These are the principal compulsory code effects, not an exhaustive inventory of Title I consequences.

verdicts.reason: The repeal removes the common prospective statutory basis, but neither continued operation until repeal nor every residual consequence is proved.
verdicts.corrected_wording: S.J. Res. 113 section 2, by functional description, removes the Title I statutory basis for prospective approval, prescription and enforcement of section 3 codes from June 14, 1935. For a command genuinely dependent solely on that basis, it supplies a statutory repeal backstop no later than that date. It does not establish the first ending of every related EO, negate earlier constitutional invalidity or exhaustion, or decide independent commands and accrued consequences.

verdicts.reason: Preserve section 5 conditions and the proviso's actual conjunction; earlier-action immunity and retroactive effect are not resolved by this record.
verdicts.corrected_wording: As enacted, section 5 exempts qualifying codes, agreements or licenses approved, prescribed or issued and in effect under Title I, and compliant action taken during the specified period, from the federal antitrust laws, with the stated sixty-day tail and license qualification. The resolution restricts the exemption to agreements and action thereunder described in numbered clauses (1) and (2), joined in the statute by and. It does not convert codes into agreements. The temporal effect on pre-repeal code actions is unresolved here. A surviving defense for prior action would not itself establish continued prospective compulsory code operation.

verdicts.reason: The described administrative acts are in the held transcriptions; EO7252 dates EO7075 and sets its own January 1, 1936 effectiveness. This judgment is limited to the section 3 code-approval scope and does not confirm EO7075's abridged text as a complete inventory.
The statute establishes a scheduled sunset, retains earlier termination language, and does not defer the separate repeal.
verdicts.corrected_wording: S.J. Res. 113 substituted April 1, 1936 as Title I's scheduled sunset while leaving section 2(c)'s earlier-emergency-termination alternative. It did not postpone the June 14 repeal of code-making and enforcement provisions. The scheduled sunset is a later statutory event for a genuinely section 3-dependent command; actual persistence and first ending of remaining authorities such as section 4(a) require their own evidence.

verdicts.reason: No actual denial order is among these shared sources. A self-executing disposition can be completed, but signature alone cannot prove all performance/effective conditions.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Where the complete operative text itself finally and unconditionally denies an exemption or dismisses a complaint, without a later act or unmet effective condition, the decisional command can be exhausted when that disposition takes effect. Establish that event from the actual instrument. Identify any stay, exception, direction or retained authority separately. Continuing code obligations derive from their own legal basis; the resolution is a later repeal event, subject to earlier invalidity and endings, not proof of the denial's performance.
